items.text: Remember that water is a liquid (l), not an aqueous solution (aq). An aqueous solution is formed when something is dissolved in water.

items.label: section_header
items.text: EXAMPLE 2

items.label: text
items.text: Balance the equation for the combustion of ethane:

items.label: formula
items.text: C _ { 2 } H _ { 6 } + O _ { 2 } \rightarrow C O _ { 2 } + H _ { 2 } O

items.label: text
items.text: Starting from the left, balance the carbons:

items.label: formula
items.text: C _ { 2 } H _ { 6 } + O _ { 2 } \rightarrow 2 C O _ { 2 } + H _ { 2 } O

items.label: text
items.text: Now the hydrogens:

items.label: formula
items.text: C _ { 2 } H _ { 6 } + O _ { 2 } \rightarrow 2 C O _ { 2 } + 3 H _ { 2 } O

items.label: text
items.text: Finally the oxygens: there are 7 oxygens ((2 × 2) + 3) on the right-hand side, but only 2 on the left. The problem is that the oxygens have to go around in pairs. So how can you obtain an odd number (7) of oxygens on the left-hand side?

items.label: text
items.text: The trick with this is to allow yourself to have halves in your equation. 7 oxygen atoms, O, is the same as 31 oxygen molecules, O2.

items.label: text
items.text: Now double everything to get rid of the half:

items.label: section_header
items.text: STATE SYMBOLS

items.label: text
items.text: State symbols are often, but not always, written after the formulae of the various substances in an equation to show what physical state everything is in. You need to know four different state symbols:

items.label: text
items.text: (s) solid (l) liquid (g) gas (aq) in aqueous solution (dissolved in water) So an equation might look like this:

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 K ( s ) + 2 H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) \rightarrow 2 K O H ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } ( g )

items.label: text
items.text: This shows that solid potassium reacts with liquid water to make a solution of potassium hydroxide in water and hydrogen gas.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HOW MUCH OF EACH SUBSTANCE REACTS IN A CHEMICAL REACTION?

items.label: text
items.text: You can make iron(ll) sulfide by heating a mixture of iron and sulfur:

items.label: formula
items.text: F e + S \rightarrow F e S

items.label: text
items.text: How do you know what proportions to mix them in? You can't just mix equal masses of them because iron and sulfur atoms don't weigh the same. Iron atoms contain more protons and neutrons than sulfur atoms, so an iron atom is one and three-quarter times heavier than a sulfur atom. In this or any other reaction, you can get the right proportions only if you know about the masses of the individual atoms that take part in the reaction.

items.text: RELATIVE ATOMIC MASS (A,)
